title: A voice becomes words.
intro: Imagine a small team inside your computer. One member listens, one understands, and one puts the words where you are typing.
story: Press the shortcut and VOCO starts listening. It turns your speech into words on your own computer and pastes them at your cursor while you are still talking. Press the shortcut again and VOCO finishes the last words.
Each part of VOCO does one job and passes small messages to the next. Sound travels in packets of one tenth of a second, so words can appear before you finish a sentence.

Nothing you say leaves the computer. The speech model runs on the processor, and the only network request asks GitHub whether a new release exists. Later chapters open each box and show the real code inside.

steps.label: Shortcut
steps.detail: You press Alt+D, or the shortcut you chose. The same shortcut, or Stop dictation in VOCO's menu, ends the recording.

steps.label: Microphone
steps.detail: VOCO records the microphone. On Wayland, Rust records through libpulse. On X11, the window records through a WebKit AudioWorklet.

steps.label: Speech model
steps.detail: A Python worker runs NVIDIA Nemotron Speech Streaming on the processor and answers with the transcript so far.

steps.label: Delivery
steps.detail: Only the new words move on. VOCO puts them on the clipboard, then presses Shift+Insert.

steps.label: Your cursor
steps.detail: The words land in whichever app has keyboard focus. VOCO never presses Enter for you.

facts.title: One warm worker
facts.text: The speech worker starts and loads its model when VOCO launches, then stays running between recordings. If it has exited, the next recording starts a fresh one.

facts.title: Words follow the focus
facts.text: VOCO doesn't remember where a recording started. Each group of words goes to whatever has keyboard focus when that group is ready.

facts.title: Local by design
facts.text: The window's content security policy allows connections only to VOCO itself, Tauri's message channel and api.github.com. Speech never needs the network.

facts.title: Stop finishes the job
facts.text: Stop sends the last audio, waits for the final transcript and pastes it. Words that couldn't be pasted are copied to the clipboard, and VOCO tells you.

files.why: Runs one recording from Start through Stop.
Sends audio packets and passes on only the new words.
Starts the speech worker and exchanges one message at a time with it.
The worker's main loop: one request in, one answer out.
Copies words to the clipboard and presses the paste key.
The app's identity, its content security policy and the Debian package contents.

caution: VOCO pastes into whatever has keyboard focus. Sending the paste keys doesn't prove that the app accepted the words.

quiz.question: You start dictating in an editor, then click into a chat window while you keep talking. Where do the next words go?
answers: Back to the editor, where the recording started
To the chat window, because it now has keyboard focus
Nowhere, because VOCO pauses when focus changes
quiz.why: VOCO pastes each group of words into whatever has keyboard focus when the group is ready. It doesn't remember where the recording started.

title: Meet the languages.
intro: VOCO is one app written in several languages. Each language sits where it fits best.
story: Rust is the part the operating system sees. It starts processes, owns files and sockets, talks to the desktop and presses the paste keys.
The window is a small React app written in TypeScript. It runs inside WebKitGTK and can reach the system only through commands that Rust registers.

Speech recognition runs in a Python worker. A small C++ bridge connects it to NeMo-Speech.cpp, the native recognizer. Two optional extensions, one for GNOME Shell and one for Chromium, are written in JavaScript.

steps.label: Rust
steps.detail: The Tauri 2 shell: processes, sockets, files, D-Bus, the tray, Wayland capture and paste.

steps.label: TypeScript
steps.detail: The React 19 window: onboarding, settings, each recording and X11 capture.

steps.label: Python
steps.detail: The speech worker reads one JSON line and writes one JSON line for each request.

steps.label: C and C++
steps.detail: native_capture_pulse.c talks to libpulse. nemo_bridge.cpp calls the recognizer.

steps.label: JavaScript
steps.detail: The GNOME companion in the top bar and the Chromium extension.

facts.title: Pinned toolchains
facts.text: CI builds with Rust 1.94.0 and the Node version in .nvmrc, which is 24. Cargo.toml pins Tauri to exactly 2.11.6.

facts.title: Messages, not shared memory
facts.text: The parts talk through Tauri commands and events, a pipe to the worker, local sockets and D-Bus. No part reaches into another's memory.

facts.title: A clean Python process
facts.text: Rust starts the worker with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, so Python writes no cache files next to the installed code.

facts.title: Where each part lives
facts.text: apps/desktop/src holds the window, apps/desktop/src-tauri the Rust shell, runtime/speech the worker, runtime/native the recognizer build and integrations the two extensions.

The GNOME Shell companion, in JavaScript.

The window's dependencies: React, TypeScript and Vite.
Repository scripts and the required Node version.

caution: The window has no shell plugin and can't start programs. It can ask only for the commands that lib.rs registers.

quiz.question: Which part starts the speech worker and the paste helpers?
answers: The React window
The GNOME companion

title: One press, one recording.
intro: A shortcut makes a small promise: one press starts a recording, and the next press finishes it.
story: The shortcut is Alt+D unless you change it. Change shortcut in VOCO's menu offers Alt+D, Alt+Shift+D and Custom shortcut…, which opens the shortcut settings. A custom shortcut needs Alt, Control or Super plus one main key.

How the key press reaches VOCO depends on the desktop. On X11, VOCO grabs the shortcut. On Wayland, VOCO reads the keyboards for the two preset shortcuts, or the GNOME companion grabs them inside the Shell.
Every route ends at the same gate. It ignores a second toggle that arrives within 120 ms of the first, so one press never counts twice.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: VOCO checks the saved shortcut at startup. An invalid one is reset to Alt+D, and VOCO tells you why.

steps.label: Route
steps.detail: The press arrives through the X11 grab, the companion's grab, keyboard reading, the VOCO Dictation IBus input source or voco --toggle.

steps.label: Consume
steps.detail: A grab keeps the keys away from other apps. Reading the keyboards only observes, so the focused app sees the keys too.

steps.label: Debounce
steps.detail: A toggle within 120 ms of the previous one is ignored.

steps.label: Toggle
steps.detail: The window starts or stops the recording. A toggle that arrives before the window is ready is kept and applied once it is.

facts.title: X11 toggles on release
facts.text: While the chord is held, VOCO's grab receives every key. VOCO waits for the release before it toggles, so the paste keys reach the app.

facts.title: Passive keys also reach the app
facts.text: When VOCO reads the keyboards, the focused app gets the shortcut as well. Browsers move the cursor to the address bar, so your words land there, and terminals delete a word. Once per launch VOCO shows "Your shortcut also reached the app" with a way to avoid it.

facts.title: One toggle, however it arrives
facts.text: The GNOME companion holds a 2.5-second lease on the shortcut, and while it is fresh VOCO ignores the same keys from the keyboards. The IBus source holds a 1-second lease, and VOCO also releases its X11 grab so the source receives the keys.

facts.title: voco --toggle
facts.text: A desktop binding can run voco --toggle. It connects once to VOCO's owner-only socket, and the connection itself is the request. It never launches VOCO, changes focus or confirms whether recording started.

facts.title: Other shortcuts on Wayland
facts.text: Keyboard reading covers only Alt+D and Alt+Shift+D, so any other shortcut on Wayland needs a desktop binding that runs voco --toggle. VOCO registers a shortcut through Tauri's global-shortcut plugin only outside Wayland, and only while no IBus source takes the chord. Whenever settings can't confirm that the shortcut works, they advise: "To dictate into other apps, start dictation from the tray or assign voco --toggle to a shortcut in your desktop settings."

facts.title: Reading keyboards
facts.text: VOCO reads the keyboards in /dev/input that have an Alt key and a D key, and watches for keyboards you plug in later. It needs read access to those devices. It skips two synthetic keyboards by name, VOCO's own virtual keyboard and the device another tool's ydotoold creates, so their keys never count as the shortcut or a held modifier.

facts.title: When nothing hears the shortcut
facts.text: If no keyboard is readable and neither the GNOME companion nor the IBus source takes Alt+D or Alt+Shift+D, the shortcut does nothing at all. 20 seconds after the keyboard reader starts, VOCO says "Your shortcut can't reach VOCO yet" once and names the fix, such as enabling the VOCO panel or assigning voco --toggle to a shortcut.

facts.title: Plain status
facts.text: Shortcut help in Settings explains the current route in plain words, for example "VOCO's GNOME panel handles this shortcut." or "A live synchronized keyboard supports the configured shortcut."

files.why: Registers the shortcut, reads keyboards on Wayland and emits the toggle.
The 120 ms gate every toggle passes, and the IBus lease.
Tracks which keys each keyboard holds and counts the keyboards that can send each preset, so unplugging one can't leave a modifier stuck.
Explains in plain words whether the shortcut can work right now.
Names the fix in the shortcut notices.
The GNOME companion's D-Bus service and its shortcut lease.
Receives the shortcut from the VOCO Dictation input source.
The IBus input source that consumes the chord and changes no text.
The owner-only socket behind voco --toggle.
Command-line options, including --toggle.
The tray menu, including Change shortcut.
Listens for the toggle event in the window.
Tells desktop and browser triggers apart.
Turns the shortcut's status into the words settings show.

caution: Reading the keyboards only observes. The companion's grab keeps the keys out of every app, and the IBus source keeps them out of IBus-aware fields.

quiz.question: On Wayland without the GNOME companion, you press Alt+D in a browser. What happens?
answers: Only VOCO sees the key press
The browser may also act on Alt+D, for example by focusing its address bar
Nothing, because VOCO blocks Alt+D on Wayland
quiz.why: Without the companion, VOCO reads the keyboards and only observes. The browser receives Alt+D too, which is why VOCO warns you once per launch.

title: Sound becomes numbers.
intro: A microphone measures tiny changes in air pressure. VOCO reads those measurements as a long list of numbers called samples.
story: On Wayland, Rust records through libpulse from PipeWire's Pulse service, which gives each source the identity VOCO needs to select it. It takes 44,100 samples per second on two channels and averages them into one.

On X11, the window records through WebKit with an AudioWorklet. If WebKit offers only the older ScriptProcessor fallback, VOCO can't confirm that it receives every sample. It shows "Dictation won't be typed" and never pastes that recording.
Silence is valid audio, so a long pause never ends a recording. VOCO stops on its own only when capture fails or after ten minutes.

steps.label: Choose a source
steps.detail: Microphone settings list every source and mark monitors of your speakers as (output monitor). VOCO uses the system default only when it is a microphone with a PipeWire identity.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: The C layer records 16-bit stereo at 44,100 Hz in 10 ms fragments.

steps.label: Mix to mono
steps.detail: On Wayland, VOCO averages the two channels into one, because the speech model needs one channel.

steps.label: Drain
steps.detail: Rust pumps the stream every 5 ms while recording, and the window collects the samples. If the window stops collecting for 5 seconds, capture ends with "Renderer drain lease expired".

steps.label: Watch health
steps.detail: If capture reports a problem, VOCO ends the recording with an error. At 600 seconds it stops normally, like pressing Stop.

facts.title: No microphone chosen yet
facts.text: VOCO still counts as ready when the system default is a microphone it can record from: the tray reads "VOCO — Ready · microphone checks on first use", and Start dictation chooses that default. Without such a default it reads "VOCO — Microphone setup required". VOCO opens no microphone until a recording or a voice test starts.

facts.title: No default microphone
facts.text: When there is no default, or the default is a monitor or has no PipeWire identity, VOCO says "No default microphone is available. Connect a microphone or choose one in Microphone settings."

facts.title: Health checks in WebKit
facts.text: Every 250 ms VOCO checks the WebKit track. It cancels the recording if the track ends, stays muted by the system for 3 seconds or delivers no samples for 5 seconds.

facts.title: The drain lease
facts.text: Only VOCO's main page may drain native capture. If the window stops draining, capture ends after 5 seconds, so a stuck window can't keep the microphone open.

facts.title: A ten-minute limit
facts.text: Both capture paths stop after 600 seconds, and the recording finishes like a normal Stop.

facts.title: The level meter
facts.text: The window computes each level from a batch of samples, the same way on every capture path. The level spans -44 to -12 dB, VOCO sends a new one at most every 40 ms, and a level older than 250 ms reads as silence.

files.why: The window's side of native capture: start, drain and stop.
Native capture's lease, pump and call timeouts.
Rust's side of the C capture layer.
Records from libpulse: 16-bit stereo at 44,100 Hz.
The commands the window uses for native capture.
The X11 AudioWorklet that forwards samples.
Opens the microphone and wires capture into a recording.
Loads the list of native sources for settings.
The WebKit health checks.
Turns samples into a meter level.
Keeps samples in memory for the Stop tail, up to the limit.
The 600-second limit both capture paths share.
Microphone settings, including monitor labels.
Finds the system default microphone VOCO can record from.
Keeps VOCO ready when no microphone is chosen yet.

caution: A long pause keeps the recording open. Press the shortcut again when you finish, or VOCO keeps listening until the ten-minute limit.

quiz.question: You pause for ten seconds in the middle of a sentence. What does VOCO do?
answers: Keeps recording, because silence is valid audio
Stops after five seconds of silence
Deletes the words so far
quiz.why: The health checks look for capture that stopped delivering samples, not for quiet. Only a capture failure or the ten-minute limit ends a recording on its own.

title: Audio on a conveyor belt.
intro: Audio doesn't wait for the end of a sentence. It moves to the speech worker in small packets, like boxes on a conveyor belt.
story: VOCO cuts the audio into packets of one tenth of a second and sends one request to the worker at a time. Each request carries the recording's session name and a number that grows by one.
Each answer holds the whole transcript so far. VOCO compares it with the previous one and passes on only the new ending. Words never change once they move on.
If recognition falls more than three seconds behind, or rewrites words it already gave, VOCO stops transcribing this recording. Words already pasted stay where they are.

steps.label: Collect
steps.detail: The stream gathers round(rate × 0.1) samples, which is 100 ms of audio at any sample rate.

steps.label: Send
steps.detail: Only one request is in flight. Newer packets wait in line.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: Each answer must carry the same session and number as its request, and the append-only mode.

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: VOCO keeps only text that extends the previous transcript.

steps.label: Paste
steps.detail: The new words go to delivery. If a paste is still running, newer words wait and go together.

facts.title: A three-second limit
facts.text: When more than three seconds of audio wait in line, VOCO stops with "Recognition fell more than three seconds behind, so VOCO stopped transcribing."

facts.title: No rewrites
facts.text: If an answer changes earlier words, VOCO stops with "Recognition revised earlier words, so VOCO stopped transcribing." Either way you see "Dictation interrupted", and the words already pasted stay.

facts.title: Three paste outcomes
facts.text: A paste that changes nothing leaves the words pending, and Stop retries them 3 times, 250 ms apart. A rejected paste, refused before the clipboard changed, stops typing. An uncertain paste also stops typing, and VOCO never sends those words again.

facts.title: Metadata, not words
facts.text: The queue reports lengths, counts and timings, never the words, and only when VOCO_PERFORMANCE_LOG=1: once Rust answers that logging is off, the window sends no reports. At most 32 reports are in flight; extra ones are dropped and counted, and Rust keeps only the fields it knows.

files.why: Packets, the one-request rule, append-only checks and the three-second limit.
Tests for revisions, backlogs and paste outcomes.
Tests for the start of a stream.
Forwards retained audio to the stream at Stop.
Keeps only known metadata fields from queue reports.

caution: Append-only is a promise about delivery, not about the model. The model may change its mind, and VOCO stops rather than edit text that is already in an app.

quiz.question: The worker's new answer changes a word VOCO already pasted. What happens?
answers: VOCO deletes the old word and pastes the new one
VOCO ignores the change and keeps pasting
VOCO stops transcribing this recording, and the pasted words stay
quiz.why: VOCO never edits text it already delivered. A revision breaks the append-only rule, so transcription stops and the pasted words stay as they are.

title: The speech worker has a rulebook.
intro: The speech worker is a separate program. VOCO and the worker follow a short rulebook, one message at a time.
story: VOCO starts one worker when it launches and keeps it warm. The two talk through a pipe: VOCO writes one line of JSON, and the worker answers with one line. The requests are start, push, finish and cancel, and a push carries at most one second of audio.
Every message is checked on both sides. If anything goes wrong, such as a timeout, a mismatched answer or a rejected request, Rust drops the worker.
A new worker starts only at the next warmup or the next recording. VOCO never sends the same request twice, so no audio is processed twice.

steps.label: Launch
steps.detail: Rust runs /usr/bin/python3 with stream_worker.py. VOCO_STREAM_PYTHON and VOCO_STREAM_WORKER may name other absolute local files. The worker has 30 seconds to load the model and report ready.

steps.label: Start
steps.detail: A start names the session, 1 to 80 characters long, and a number that is 0 or more.

steps.label: Push
steps.detail: Each push carries at most one second of mono audio at 8,000 to 96,000 Hz. The rate stays the same for the whole session, and every value must be a finite number.

steps.label: Answer
steps.detail: The worker answers within 10 seconds. A push returns text only when the transcript changed; a finish always returns the final text.

steps.label: Close
steps.detail: A finish or cancel ends the session. Each request's number must be larger than the last.

facts.title: Bounded messages
facts.text: A request may be at most 4 MiB and an answer at most 1 MiB. Anything larger is refused.

facts.title: Clean output
facts.text: stream_worker.py keeps library messages off the protocol, so only answers travel on the worker's output.

facts.title: The thread rule
facts.text: The worker uses one less than the processors it may run on, between 1 and 4, to leave room for capture, the compositor and the app you are typing into. NEMO_SPEECH_CPU_THREADS overrides it.

facts.title: No replay
facts.text: If the worker dies during a recording, the next push or finish gets "worker lost". Transcription ends for that recording, and the next recording starts a new worker.

facts.title: Private diagnostics
facts.text: When the worker rejects a request, its answer names only the error type after "stream request rejected: ". It never contains audio or text.

files.why: Starts the worker, enforces time limits and never replays a request.
The worker's entry point; keeps library output off the protocol.
Checks every request and answers one line at a time.
Checks audio packets and runs the silence gate.
Tests for the rulebook.
Tests for the thread rule.

caution: The worker's answer says what the model heard, not what reached an app. Delivery is a separate step with its own outcomes.

quiz.question: The worker crashes in the middle of a recording. What happens?
answers: VOCO restarts it and replays the audio
Transcription stops for this recording, and the next recording starts a new worker
VOCO keeps pasting from its own copy of the model
quiz.why: Rust never replays a request. A push or finish without a worker gets "worker lost", and a new worker starts only at the next warmup or recording.

title: How the model guesses words.
intro: A speech model doesn't look words up. It makes a careful guess from patterns it learned, and the guess grows as you speak.
story: VOCO uses NVIDIA Nemotron Speech Streaming, an English model with 0.6 billion parameters, stored at 8-bit precision in a GGUF file. It runs on the processor through NeMo-Speech.cpp and needs no graphics card.
The model is built for streaming. It listens in short chunks and keeps a growing guess of the transcript, with punctuation.
Before loading, the worker checks the file's SHA-256 fingerprint. If it doesn't match the pinned value, the worker refuses to start.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: The worker computes the model file's SHA-256 and compares it with the pinned value. A mismatch stops the worker before the model loads.

steps.label: Load
steps.detail: The recognizer loads with its right-context setting at 1. VOCO_NEMOTRON_CONTEXT accepts 0 or 1.

steps.label: Warm up
steps.detail: Before the first recording, the worker runs one second of zeros at 16,000 Hz through the recognizer.

steps.label: Gate
steps.detail: Long runs of exact digital zeros are skipped. The gate keeps 640 ms before sound and 1.5 seconds after it.

steps.label: Transcribe
steps.detail: The recognizer returns its finished text joined with its latest partial guess.

facts.title: A pinned build
facts.text: NATIVE-BUILD.json records the NeMo-Speech.cpp and ggml revisions and the patch digests. The build targets generic x86-64 with AVX, AVX2, FMA and F16C, and leaves AVX-512, AMX and OpenMP off. That sets the processor VOCO needs.

facts.title: Two small patches
facts.text: One patch lets the first chunk start without waiting for another 90 ms of audio. The other runs 1 to 16 threads in a pool that sleeps between steps instead of spinning.

facts.title: Fewer, larger frames
facts.text: When the gate releases audio it held back, the worker joins those packets into frames of at most one second, without changing any samples.

facts.title: Original samples
facts.text: The recognizer always receives the original samples at the capture rate, and each push names that rate.

facts.title: Turning the gate off
facts.text: VOCO_SILENCE_GATE=off disables the gate. The default mode, zero, treats a packet as quiet only when every sample is exactly zero. Any other value stops the worker before the model loads.

files.why: Checks the model fingerprint and loads the native library.
The bridge into NeMo-Speech.cpp.
The warmup, the silence gate and frame joining.
The request loop and the thread rule.
The model's source, revision and fingerprint.
Pinned revisions, patch digests and processor flags.
Builds the native recognizer from pinned source.
Bounded threads that sleep between steps.
Lets the first chunk start without extra audio.

caution: The transcript is the model's best guess. VOCO checks that the model file is the right one, not that each word is right.

quiz.question: Someone replaces the model file with a different one. What happens?
answers: The worker refuses it because the fingerprint doesn't match
VOCO downloads a fresh copy
The worker loads it and transcribes as usual
quiz.why: The worker compares the file's SHA-256 with the pinned value before loading. VOCO never downloads models, so a mismatch stops the worker.

title: Words meet the cursor.
intro: The last step puts words into another app. VOCO does it the way you would: copy, then paste.
story: insertion.rs pastes one group of words at a time. It puts the words on the clipboard, then presses Shift+Insert. In the code's words, "Shift+Insert is the paste key shared by GTK, Qt, Chromium, Firefox, Electron and terminal emulators."

Terminals paste the PRIMARY selection instead of the clipboard, so VOCO fills both. Before each paste it checks the helper programs and, on Wayland, its own virtual keyboard, and it waits for you to release the shortcut's keys.
An optional Chromium extension offers a second route. In a tab where you enable it, VOCO inserts words at the caret of one plain text field, and the extension confirms each insert with a receipt.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: The text must be 1 to 100,000 bytes and the helpers ready. On Wayland the virtual keyboard must exist, and this session must be the active one.

steps.label: Clean
steps.detail: Control characters, including newlines and tabs, become spaces, so a terminal never receives Enter.

steps.label: Settle
steps.detail: VOCO waits until 150 ms have passed since the previous paste, so that app can read the clipboard first.

steps.label: Copy
steps.detail: The words go to CLIPBOARD, then PRIMARY. A PRIMARY failure only logs a warning.

steps.label: Press
steps.detail: VOCO waits up to 1.5 seconds for the shortcut's modifier keys to be released, then sends Shift+Insert.

facts.title: A separate leading space
facts.text: When new words start with VOCO's joining space, that space goes out as its own Space key before the paste, because Chromium's address bar strips pasted leading spaces.

facts.title: Three failure outcomes
facts.text: No change: no keys were sent, so the words wait for the next try. Rejected: VOCO refused before touching the clipboard, and typing stops. Uncertain: a helper failed after it started, or the paste keys failed after the copy, so typing stops and VOCO never sends those words again.

facts.title: Checked before recording
facts.text: If a helper is missing, or on Wayland the virtual keyboard can't be used, the recording doesn't start. VOCO shows "Dictation setup incomplete" with the reason.

facts.title: Only the active session types
facts.text: A virtual keyboard types into whichever login owns the screen. So on Wayland VOCO asks logind before the copy and again just before the keys. When logind reports this session as not active, as after switching to another user, VOCO reports "This desktop session isn't the active one, so VOCO sent no paste keys." If logind can't answer, VOCO doesn't block.

facts.title: VOCO steps aside
facts.text: If VOCO's own window is showing when you start, VOCO hides it instead of recording and shows "VOCO hidden" with "Click where you want the text, then start dictation again."

facts.title: The browser route
facts.text: The Chromium extension works through its toolbar button and Alt+Shift+V. It inserts only into a text area or a text, search, URL or telephone input with a collapsed caret. It skips disabled and read-only fields, fields inside a private or inert area, and fields whose autocomplete asks for a password, a one-time code or payment details. Incognito tabs are refused, and an insert counts only when a matching receipt comes back.

facts.title: The clipboard keeps the words
facts.text: VOCO doesn't restore what the clipboard held before. After dictation, the clipboard holds the last words VOCO pasted.

VOCO's own keyboard for the Wayland paste keys.

Hands new words to delivery one group at a time.
Runs helper programs within bounds and tells a failed start apart from a failure after the helper may have acted.

quiz.question: A paste helper fails after it started. Why doesn't VOCO simply try again?
answers: The keys may already have reached the app, so a retry could type the words twice
Helpers can run only once per recording
VOCO retries silently in the background
quiz.why: After a helper starts, the clipboard or the app may already hold the words. VOCO marks the paste uncertain and never replays it.

title: Stop means finish the work.
intro: Pressing Stop doesn't throw away the end of your sentence. VOCO finishes the work before it goes quiet.
story: When you stop, VOCO flushes the microphone and sends the audio the worker hasn't heard yet, including the last partial packet. Then it asks for the final transcript and pastes the last words.
If some words couldn't be pasted, VOCO copies them to the clipboard and tells you. If even the copy fails, the words wait in Review.
A recognition failure is different. VOCO copies nothing, because the transcript may be missing words, and asks you to check your text field.

steps.label: Flush
steps.detail: On X11 the AudioWorklet must confirm its flush within 80 ms. Otherwise VOCO says "The end of this recording could not be confirmed, so VOCO did not finish it. Try again."

steps.label: Forward the tail
steps.detail: VOCO sends the retained samples the stream hasn't received, then the partial packet.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: The worker returns the final transcript. Words still pending get up to 3 more paste attempts, 250 ms apart.

steps.label: Deliver or copy
steps.detail: Words left over go to CLIPBOARD and PRIMARY, joining space included, and VOCO shows "Dictation copied to clipboard".

steps.label: Clean up
steps.detail: VOCO clears the audio from memory and deletes the recording's journal entry.

facts.title: Typing stopped, listening continues
facts.text: When a paste is rejected or uncertain, VOCO shows "VOCO stopped typing" with "It's still listening. When you stop, VOCO copies the rest of your words to the clipboard."

facts.title: After an uncertain paste

facts.title: When recognition fails
facts.text: VOCO shows "Dictation interrupted" with "Some words may be missing. Check your text field before starting again." If no words were recognized yet, the message starts "Nothing was typed." and gives the reason instead. Nothing is copied.

facts.text: When WebKit offered only the ScriptProcessor fallback, VOCO already showed "Dictation won't be typed". At Stop it clears the audio, and the window shows "VOCO couldn't confirm it received all of your audio, so it didn't type this recording. Try again."

answers: Types them with simulated key presses
Copies them to the clipboard and tells you to paste them
Discards them

title: When something goes wrong.
intro: Computers crash sometimes. VOCO keeps a small private note of what you said, so a crash doesn't lose your words.
story: While you dictate, VOCO writes the transcript, and only the transcript, to a journal on disk. A normal finish deletes the entry, and so do Quit and a clean shutdown signal.
If VOCO exits unexpectedly, the entry stays. At the next start VOCO moves it to Review, where it waits for you.
Review opens only when you choose it from VOCO's menu. You can copy each transcript or discard it, and Review never pastes anything by itself.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Each new result updates the recording's entry. An entry larger than 256 KiB is refused.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: A normal finish deletes the entry.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: At the next start, an unfinished entry moves to Review. If only the window reloads, it moves at once.

steps.label: Keep five
steps.detail: Review keeps up to five entries and removes the oldest.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: Copy transcript puts the text on the clipboard. Discard first asks "Discard this transcript?" and offers Keep or Discard transcript.

facts.title: Owner-only files

facts.title: When the journal is unavailable
facts.text: Dictation still works. VOCO shows "Crash recovery unavailable" with "Dictation continues, but VOCO can't recover it if VOCO exits unexpectedly."

facts.title: Clean exits clean up
facts.text: Quit VOCO, SIGINT and SIGTERM delete the active entry, because those exits are chosen, not crashes.

facts.title: Review is explicit
facts.text: Each entry is "Kept until you discard it." VOCO never opens, pastes or retries recovered text for you.

facts.title: Cleanup failures
facts.text: If temporary text can't be deleted, VOCO says "Temporary dictation text could not be deleted. VOCO will retry cleanup before the next recording."

quiz.question: VOCO crashes in the middle of a recording. What happens to the words you said?
answers: They are pasted automatically at the next start
They are lost, because the journal is deleted
They wait in Review until you open it from VOCO's menu
quiz.why: An unexpected exit leaves the journal entry in place. At the next start VOCO moves it to Review, which opens only when you choose it and never pastes by itself.

title: A small interface, clear ownership.
intro: VOCO has few settings, and one part owns them. That keeps the file simple and safe.
story: VOCO stores five settings in one file, and Rust owns it. The window sends small changes, called patches, and Rust refuses fields it doesn't know and null values.
Fields from older versions are ignored and dropped at the next save. If VOCO can't read the file, it never overwrites it. Dictation pauses, and a recovery panel offers three ways out.
Only Reset keeps a backup of the old file.

steps.label: Load
steps.detail: Rust reads $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/voco/config.json.

steps.label: Migrate
steps.detail: If that file doesn't exist, VOCO copies $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/voice/config.json when present.

steps.label: Patch
steps.detail: The window sends only the fields that changed. Unknown fields and null values are refused.

steps.label: Save
steps.detail: Rust writes the file atomically. The folder is 0700 and the file 0600, so only you can read them.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: When the file can't be read, the recovery panel offers Retry loading settings, Open config directory and Reset to defaults.

facts.title: Five fields
facts.text: hotkey, which defaults to Alt+D; selectedMic; onboardingCompleted; updateChannel; and installChannel.

facts.title: Update checks
facts.text: VOCO checks after startup and when you change the update channel. It reuses an answer younger than 6 hours, and otherwise asks GitHub for the 12 newest releases, with a 15-second timeout. Check for updates in Settings always asks.

facts.title: Only a notice
facts.text: When a newer release exists, VOCO shows an "Update available" notification once for that release, and Settings offers Open latest release. VOCO never downloads or installs anything.

facts.title: Two channels
facts.text: The default channel ignores pre-releases, and its helper text reads "Recommended for everyday use." Beta includes them: "Beta releases change more often." Drafts are always ignored.

facts.title: Installation method
facts.text: installChannel only chooses which update instructions VOCO shows.

facts.title: Reset is confirmed
facts.text: Reset to defaults asks "Reset local settings?" and needs Confirm reset before it replaces the file.

caution: Settings stay on this computer. VOCO has no account and syncs nothing.

quiz.question: The window sends a patch with a field Rust doesn't know. What happens?
answers: Rust refuses the change
Rust saves it for later versions
Rust drops that field and saves the rest
quiz.why: Rust owns the file and accepts only the five fields it knows. A patch with an unknown field is refused, so nothing unexpected reaches the file.

title: One app, several Linux paths.
intro: A Linux desktop is made of many parts. VOCO fits into them with a few small, private pieces.
story: Only one copy of VOCO runs per login. Launching it again brings the running copy forward and never starts a recording.
Other programs reach VOCO through private sockets that check the caller's user ID. Notifications go through D-Bus, the desktop's message bus.

On Wayland, VOCO presses the paste keys through its own virtual keyboard. A udev rule in the package lets the person at the computer use /dev/uinput, so there is no service, daemon or group to set up.

steps.label: Lock
steps.detail: instance.lock in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/voco makes sure only one copy runs.

steps.label: Activate
steps.detail: A second launch connects to voco-activate.sock and asks the running copy to show itself, waiting at most 2 seconds.

steps.label: Trigger
steps.detail: voco.sock and voice.sock sit in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or in a private voco-<uid> folder in the temporary directory when that variable is unset. The sockets are 0600, and a connection is the request.

steps.label: Notify
steps.detail: Notifications go through D-Bus with a 3-second timeout.

steps.label: Keyboard
steps.detail: On Wayland, VOCO creates its virtual keyboard at startup and keeps it until it quits.

facts.title: Command-line options
facts.text: voco accepts --toggle, --check-desktop-input, --check-panel, --setup-panel, --version and --help. Unknown arguments exit with code 2.

facts.title: A hidden window
facts.text: With native capture VOCO really hides its window. On X11, where WebKit records, VOCO instead shrinks the window to 1 by 1 pixel and moves it off-screen.

facts.title: Checking input
facts.text: voco --check-desktop-input checks the paste prerequisites without launching VOCO or sending keys: the clipboard helper, xdotool on X11, and on Wayland that /dev/uinput opens for reading and writing. It exits with code 1 when something is missing.

facts.title: Access from a udev rule
facts.text: 70-voco-uinput.rules tags /dev/uinput with uaccess, so logind gives the user of the active local session access through an ACL that follows seat changes. voco-uinput.conf loads the uinput module at boot.

facts.title: A leftover service
facts.text: At a Wayland start, VOCO removes a leftover link to voco-ydotoold.service from this login's systemd folder, but only if the link points at /usr/lib/systemd/user/voco-ydotoold.service and that file no longer exists. Then it stops the unit and reloads the user manager, off the startup path.

facts.title: Two packages, one tree
facts.text: The Debian package depends on xclip, xdotool and wl-clipboard, among others, and recommends nothing. The Fedora RPM is built from the same staged files and requires the same packages under their Fedora names.

quiz.question: VOCO is already running and you launch it again from the app menu. What happens?
answers: The running copy shows itself, and no recording starts
A second copy starts
The running copy starts recording
quiz.why: The instance lock keeps one copy per login. A second launch asks the running copy to show itself through voco-activate.sock and never toggles dictation.

title: Draw the trust boundaries.
intro: Privacy is easier to check when you can see where each piece of data goes. VOCO keeps the map short.
story: Audio stays in memory while you record and is cleared when the recording ends. It travels to the worker over a private pipe, never over the network.
Text lives briefly in the crash journal and on the clipboard. The window may connect only to VOCO itself and GitHub's release API.
Logs are off by default. When you turn them on, they hold metadata such as lengths and timings, never your words or audio.

steps.label: Microphone
steps.detail: VOCO opens the microphone only for a recording or a voice test.

steps.label: Worker
steps.detail: Audio and text travel to the worker through its standard input and output.

steps.label: Sockets
steps.detail: VOCO's sockets are owner-only, and the trigger, activation, IBus and browser sockets check the caller's user ID through one shared helper.

steps.label: Files
steps.detail: Settings, the journal and logs are private to your user.

steps.label: Network
steps.detail: The only request asks GitHub's API about new releases.

facts.title: Opt-in logs
facts.text: VOCO_PERFORMANCE_LOG=1 and VOCO_HOTKEY_TRACE=1 turn on metadata logs. They never record dictated text, audio or window titles.

facts.title: Debug audio
facts.text: Saving audio needs three variables, VOCO_DEV_NATIVE_CAPTURE, VOCO_DEBUG_CAPTURE_AUDIO and VOCO_DEBUG_NATIVE_CAPTURE, all set to exactly 1. Then VOCO writes one owner-only bundle in $XDG_STATE_HOME/voco/debug-native-captures after the recording.

facts.title: The clipboard is shared
facts.text: Other apps can read the clipboard. VOCO pastes through it and doesn't restore what it held before.

facts.title: No shell access
facts.text: The window has no shell plugin. Its permissions are Tauri's core defaults and a list of window controls, so it can't register global shortcuts either.

facts.title: Browser limits
facts.text: The Chromium extension refuses incognito tabs, skips password, one-time-code and payment fields, and works only in tabs where you enable it.

facts.title: Paste keys for one person
facts.text: The package's uaccess rule gives /dev/uinput to the user of the active local session alone, with no group, daemon or socket. VOCO's keyboard can press only Shift, Insert and Space, and VOCO sends keys only while its own session is the active one.

facts.title: Same user, not same program
facts.text: The sockets keep out other users. They are not a boundary against a compromised program that runs as you.

answers: It uploads audio for better recognition

quiz.why: Speech runs on the computer, and the content security policy allows only VOCO itself, Tauri's message channel and api.github.com. The update check is the only request.

title: Measure the right stopwatch.
intro: A time is only useful when you know where the stopwatch starts and stops. VOCO's measurements always say which clock they use.
story: Performance logging is off until you turn it on. Then VOCO and the worker record timings and resource use, never words or audio.
report-performance.py summarizes the log with counts, medians, 95th percentiles and maximums, and never scores what it didn't measure.
A replay script feeds pinned public speech to the real worker, so one machine can be measured again under the same conditions.

steps.label: Opt in
steps.detail: Set VOCO_PERFORMANCE_LOG=1 before starting VOCO.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: VOCO writes performance.jsonl up to 8 MiB, then keeps one previous file. It samples resource use every 2 seconds.

steps.label: Worker timings
steps.detail: The worker writes worker.jsonl up to 8 MiB and keeps 3 older files.

steps.label: Summarize
steps.detail: report-performance.py and report-speech-performance.py turn the logs into counts and percentiles.

steps.label: Replay
steps.detail: evaluate-dictation-worker.py replays public speech into the worker without opening any audio or input device.

facts.title: Logging never blocks speech
facts.text: Log records wait in a queue of 256. When it is full, VOCO drops the record and counts it rather than slow dictation.

facts.title: Named failures
facts.text: Queue failures are logged by name, such as backlog_limit and prefix_revision, with a hashed session instead of the session itself.

facts.title: Threads
facts.text: By default the worker uses at most 4 threads, one less than the processors it may use.

facts.title: Know what is measured
facts.text: Each quality record names its clock_domain and counts samples at queue_ingress, where audio enters the queue. The replay measures the worker's process boundary, not capture, the receiving app or the screen.

facts.title: Descriptive statistics
facts.text: Percentiles use the nearest-rank method and keep their sample counts. A few runs describe those runs, nothing more.

files.why: The opt-in log, its bounded queue and fixed fields.
The worker's timing log.
Sends queue metadata when logging is on.
Summarizes VOCO's performance log.
Summarizes the worker's log; missing measurements stay unavailable.
Matches queue and dispatch records without guessing what an app received.
Replays pinned public speech into the real worker.
Scores replay results with descriptive statistics.
The bounded thread pool that sleeps between steps.

caution: Compare timings only when they use the same clock, the same audio and the same machine.

quiz.question: You add two seconds of silence before the first word. Which delay grows?
answers: Time from the start of playback to the words in the field
Time from the start of speech to the words in the field
Neither, because VOCO skips silence
quiz.why: A stopwatch that starts at playback includes the silence, and one that starts at speech doesn't. That's why every timing must say where its clock starts.

title: Tests are little promises.
intro: A test is a promise written as code: when this happens, VOCO does that. Running the tests checks that the promises still hold.
story: npm test runs scripts/test-unit.sh, the fast checks that need no microphone, speech model or desktop session.

CI runs on every push and pull request to master, in seven jobs. Some start the real app in private desktop sessions and paste into real applications, and one runs the speech runtime in Debian 13 and Fedora 44 containers.
Tests use only public or synthetic audio. No personal recording is part of any test.

steps.label: Unit checks
steps.detail: scripts/test-unit.sh checks the patched libraries, the speech reports and runtime, capture helpers, the IBus engine and the window's Vitest suite.

steps.label: Rust checks
steps.detail: cargo fmt, clippy with warnings treated as errors, and cargo test.

steps.label: Speech checks
steps.detail: CI reuses the native speech runtime from a released package, checked against a fixed checksum, then runs the speech baseline and the worker protocol tests, on Ubuntu 24.04 and in the Debian 13 and Fedora 44 containers.

steps.label: Application checks
steps.detail: A release build runs end to end in private sessions: the GNOME panel, capture and paste into a focused field, the Wayland lifecycle and Chromium. On GNOME Wayland its paste keys go through VOCO's real virtual keyboard.

steps.label: Audit
steps.detail: RustSec checks the Rust dependencies, and npm run verify:security checks the JavaScript ones.

facts.title: Seven CI jobs
facts.text: Code Guide, RustSec Audit, Frontend Checks, Rust Check & Test, Application, GNOME 50 Companion, and a runtime job that runs once for Debian 13 and once for Fedora 44.

facts.title: Private sessions
facts.text: The hosted desktop tests refuse to run outside GitHub Actions, so they never touch a developer's own session.

facts.title: Many apps, one paste
facts.text: test-application-delivery.py pastes with the one production chord and reads the result back from each application itself.

facts.title: A bridge for the paste keys
facts.text: The Wayland delivery suites give their private session /dev/uinput but no /dev/input. A test-only bridge outside the session grabs each device named VOCO virtual keyboard, so its keys reach no real desktop, and replays them in order into the session's display. It accepts only the paste gesture and refuses to run beside a graphical login.

facts.title: GNOME 50, headless
facts.text: GNOME 50 has no nested mode, so the companion regression runs Shell headless on Ubuntu 26.04 and sends keys and clicks through a private RemoteDesktop session.

facts.title: Each distribution's names
facts.text: The Debian 13 and Fedora 44 jobs install VOCO's package dependencies by that distribution's names, as distro-dependencies.py prints them, so a renamed package fails in CI before a release.

facts.title: What CI never does
facts.text: Hosted CI never assembles or signs the NVIDIA package. The maintainer does that locally with assemble-release.sh.

facts.title: The guide checks itself
facts.text: The Code Guide job runs this guide's own tests: chapters, catalog and server safety.

title: How source becomes an app.
intro: Shipping turns source code into a package someone can trust. Each step leaves proof that the next step can check.
story: A release starts from a signed tag on a commit that already passed CI on master. The build runs from a clean tree, and its timestamps come from the last commit.
The build adds the speech runtime and model to a Debian package, builds a Fedora RPM from the same staged files, checks both and signs the checksums.
The installer runs the chain backwards. It checks the signature, then the checksum, and only then installs.

steps.label: Tag
steps.detail: assemble-release.sh needs a signed voco.<version> tag that git verify-tag accepts, on a commit that passed CI on master.

steps.label: Build
steps.detail: The tree must be clean, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH comes from the last commit, and the build must not change tracked files.

steps.label: Package
steps.detail: package-nvidia.py adds the speech runtime and model to the Tauri package and, with --rpm, builds the RPM from the same staged tree. verify-deb-package.sh and verify-rpm-package.sh check them.

steps.label: Sign
steps.detail: sign-release-checksums.sh signs the checksum files.

steps.label: Install
steps.detail: The install script checks the signature with gpgv, then the package checksum, then installs with APT or DNF.

facts.title: Nothing is uploaded
facts.text: assemble-release.sh ends with the assembled, signed files and prints the gh release create command with --draft and --verify-tag. A person uploads the release.

facts.title: Checking a download
facts.text: verify-release.sh exits 0 when the files are signed and verified, 1 on an integrity failure or unsafe path, and 2 when the checksums match but no usable signature exists.

facts.title: The installer
facts.text: It supports x86-64 only. It uses APT when apt-get and dpkg-query exist, otherwise DNF when dnf and rpm do, and the package manager must then report exactly that release. After installing, it checks desktop input with voco --check-desktop-input; if that fails, it says "VOCO is installed. Desktop setup needs one more step." and exits with code 2.

facts.title: Before the download
facts.text: The installer stops early on a system VOCO can't run on: glibc older than 2.39, or a processor without AVX2, FMA and F16C. It refuses only what it could read and found short, and leaves the rest to the package manager.

facts.title: One installer file
facts.text: install embeds scripts/lib/install-common.sh, the steps setup.sh also sources, byte for byte. sync-installer-ui.py --check fails on any difference.

facts.title: Same files in both
facts.text: Given the Debian package too, verify-rpm-package.sh proves that both carry the same files and that the RPM requires each Debian dependency under its Fedora name.

facts.title: A pinned install line
facts.text: The README's install line stays pinned to the release named in packaging/published-release.json, and rehearse-release.sh checks that the documented lines match.

facts.title: One script per package
facts.text: The Debian package's only maintainer script repairs directory modes from older installs, without following links or touching user data, then applies the uinput rule: it loads uinput, reloads udev's rules and re-triggers /dev/uinput, each step best effort within 10 seconds. debian_maintainer.py generates and verifies it. The RPM's only scriptlet, post.sh, runs the same three steps.

title: Borrowed code needs care.
intro: VOCO builds on libraries other people wrote. A few need small fixes, so VOCO keeps patched copies and checks them.
story: Three Rust libraries are patched in vendor: glib, global-hotkey and tray-icon. Cargo.toml tells every part of VOCO to use those copies.

Each patch is small and has one reason: in glib a security fix, in global-hotkey an X11 shortcut actor that waits for events instead of polling, and in tray-icon icons that stay valid while VOCO runs. The package carries each one's licenses and patch notes.
Scripts check each patched copy against its recorded origin, so a later update can't quietly bring back the unpatched code.

steps.detail: 0.18.5 with the two-line upstream fix for RUSTSEC-2024-0429.

steps.label: global-hotkey
steps.detail: 0.8.0 with an event-driven X11 actor.

steps.label: tray-icon
steps.detail: 0.24.2 with a Linux call that sets icons by file path.

steps.label: Ship
steps.detail: package-nvidia.py copies each crate's licenses, patch notes and provenance into /usr/share/doc/voco/vendor, and stops if one is missing.

facts.title: One glib for everyone
facts.text: GTK 0.18 and WebKit2GTK need glib 0.18, so VOCO patches Cargo's resolution and every glib user gets the fixed copy. verify-glib-backport.py checks the source against the pinned archive and the exact upstream fix, and that only one glib resolves.

facts.title: Why the X11 actor waits
facts.text: The patched global-hotkey waits on the X11 connection and a command signal instead of a timer, so key events never wait for a 50 ms tick and an idle actor never wakes. VOCO and Tauri's shortcut plugin must share this one copy.

facts.title: Why icons stay put
facts.text: The patch adds set_icon_path. VOCO writes 3 state icons and 64 meter frames into a private folder once and keeps them while it runs, so a slow tray reader can still open any icon VOCO announced.

facts.title: Licenses travel along
facts.text: The RPM marks those notices as licenses, so they stay installed even when documentation is skipped.

facts.title: Everything else is unpatched
facts.text: Other crates come from crates.io at the versions Cargo.lock records. The virtual keyboard, for example, uses evdev 0.13.2 as published.

title: Open any piece of the code.
intro: Reading a large project is easier with a thread to follow. Pick one event and follow it from file to file.
story: Follow the toggle. Rust emits voco:toggle-dictation from lib.rs. useGlobalShortcut.ts hears it, useDictation.ts and dictationRecording.ts start the recording, and dictationStream.ts sends audio through the speech_stream command.
From there, speech_stream.rs talks to the worker, and insertion.rs pastes the words. Tests sit next to the code they check, usually in a file with test in its name.
All source files lists every tracked file at the commit this guide records, so the code you read matches the chapters.

title: A microphone in the top bar.
intro: On GNOME, VOCO can live in the top bar near the clock, with bars that move while you speak.
story: The optional companion for GNOME 46, 48 and 50 shows VOCO's microphone in the top bar. While you dictate, a seven-bar meter opens on its left when there is room beside the clock.

The installer runs voco --setup-panel, and VOCO's setup and Help offer Enable live panel. Enabling adds only this extension, may need you to sign out and back in, and never restarts the Shell. The package alone never enables it, and voco --check-panel changes nothing.
Once the companion attaches, VOCO hides its tray icon. On Wayland the companion grabs Alt+D or Alt+Shift+D inside the Shell, so other apps never see the shortcut.

steps.label: Enable
steps.detail: voco --setup-panel or Enable live panel turns on this one extension for your user.

steps.label: Attach
steps.detail: The companion calls Attach over D-Bus. VOCO accepts it only from the process that owns org.gnome.Shell, then hides the tray icon.

steps.label: Poll
steps.detail: The companion asks for VOCO's state every 50 ms while recording and every 1500 ms otherwise.

steps.label: Grab
steps.detail: On Wayland it grabs the configured preset and renews a 2.5-second lease about once a second.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: If GetState stops arriving for more than 5 seconds, or the companion calls Detach, VOCO drops the lease and shows the tray icon again.

facts.title: The menu
facts.text: A primary click stops dictation, or opens VOCO when nothing can be stopped. Other mouse buttons, the Menu key and Shift+F10 open a menu with Settings, Review and Stop dictation.

facts.title: Motion
facts.text: Bars grow in 45 ms and shrink in 100 ms. While VOCO processes, the bars hold at 0.35 and pulse over 700 ms, each bar 40 ms after the last. The meter opens in 220 ms. When GNOME's animations are off, every change happens at once and nothing pulses.

facts.title: The bar formula
facts.text: Each bar's height is 0.15 + 0.85 × level × weight, with weights 0.35, 0.65, 0.9, 1, 0.8, 0.55 and 0.3 from left to right.

facts.title: Fresh levels only
facts.text: A level older than 250 ms reads as silence, so the bars never freeze on an old value.

facts.title: Keys released
facts.text: When VOCO can't read the keyboards, it asks the companion through ModifiersClear whether the shortcut's keys are up before a Wayland paste.

facts.title: Setup messages
facts.text: Active: "Live panel bars and Stop are active." Disabled: "Enable live microphone bars and the VOCO menu in your top panel." After enabling: "Panel enabled. Sign out and back in to load it; saving your work first is recommended."

facts.title: Other desktops
facts.text: On other GNOME versions: "The VOCO panel supports GNOME 46, 48 and 50. Dictation still works, but without the panel the focused app also receives Alt+D and Alt+Shift+D. To avoid that, choose another shortcut in VOCO and configure it in your desktop to run voco --toggle." On other desktops: "Use the VOCO tray menu for status and Stop. Labels depend on your desktop."

facts.title: On GNOME 50
facts.text: GNOME 50 has no Meta.is_wayland_compositor, so the companion treats a Shell without it as Wayland. Its panel button opens the menu from a click gesture, so the companion leaves primary presses and touches to the pill, and a primary click still stops dictation or opens VOCO.

facts.title: No icon at all
facts.text: The tray icon needs a tray host, on GNOME an AppIndicator extension, which Debian and Fedora don't turn on. If 20 seconds after startup the companion isn't attached and no tray host owns org.kde.StatusNotifierWatcher, VOCO says "VOCO has no icon in the top bar" once. On GNOME it adds "Open VOCO from the app menu, choose Enable live panel in Help, then sign out and back in."

facts.title: The tray fallback
facts.text: Without the companion, the tray shows 3 state icons and, while you dictate, animates 64 meter frames every 90 ms.

facts.title: The check cache
facts.text: VOCO reuses a panel check for 20 seconds, or for 2 seconds after a failed check.

title: Each desktop, its own helpers.
intro: Linux desktops differ in how programs may read keys and send them. VOCO picks a helper for each job from the session it runs in.
story: VOCO reads XDG_SESSION_TYPE. If it says wayland, VOCO takes the Wayland path; anything else takes the X11 path.

On Wayland, keys go through VOCO's own virtual keyboard, a uinput device named VOCO virtual keyboard. On GNOME with an X display, xclip sets the clipboard through XWayland: GNOME lacks the wlroots data-control protocol, wl-copy's temporary focus surface can stall, and XWayland bridges the clipboard without taking focus. Other Wayland desktops use wl-copy.
On X11, xdotool sends the keys and xclip sets the clipboard. The table below shows each combination.

steps.label: Detect
steps.detail: XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland selects the Wayland path. Any other value, or none, selects X11.

steps.label: Shortcut
steps.detail: On X11 VOCO grabs the chord. On Wayland the GNOME companion grabs it, or VOCO reads the keyboards for the two presets.

steps.label: Keys
steps.detail: On Wayland VOCO presses Shift+Insert, after a joining Space when one is needed, through its virtual keyboard. X11 uses xdotool.

steps.label: Clipboard
steps.detail: xclip on X11 and on GNOME with DISPLAY set, wl-copy on other Wayland sessions.

steps.label: Paste
steps.detail: Every path ends with Shift+Insert into the focused app.

facts.title: One keyboard for the whole run
facts.text: VOCO creates the keyboard at startup and keeps it until it quits, never one per paste. The compositor adds a new device late and could miss its first keys, so a keyboard younger than 500 ms waits before it types. When VOCO exits, the kernel removes the device and releases any key it held.

facts.title: Three keys, one at a time
facts.text: The keyboard declares only Shift, Insert and Space. Each press and release goes out in its own report, 12 ms apart, so every toolkit sees the chord in order and a paste still takes under 100 ms.

facts.title: Access without a helper
facts.text: The package's udev rule gives the user of the active local session access to /dev/uinput. To check it, voco --check-desktop-input only opens /dev/uinput; it never creates the device or sends keys. Without access it says "VOCO can't open /dev/uinput, so it can't send the paste keys. Sign out and back in once after installing VOCO; if that doesn't help, see Platform support: Access to /dev/uinput."

facts.title: Only this session types
facts.text: Keys reach whichever login owns the seat, so VOCO asks logind before the copy and again just before the keys, and sends nothing while logind reports this session as not active.

facts.title: After a key error
facts.text: If the keyboard stops accepting keys, VOCO releases Shift and drops the device, and the next paste creates a fresh one.

facts.title: Keys stay on Wayland
facts.text: Even when xclip sets the clipboard on GNOME, the paste keys still go through the virtual keyboard.
